dataset.name: 2017 Meander C sediment characterization from the East River, Colorado
description: This dataset includes characterization data collected on sediment samples from Meander C as part of the Watershed Function Scientific Focus Area (SFA) located in the Upper Colorado River Basin. The data were collected to investigate the nature of mineral-organic associations across the meander transect and with depth. Samples were collected in 2017, and analyzed using sequential extractions (water, pyrophosphate, HCl, and dithionite) and density fractionation. Data collected include: texture, pH, root biomass, and metals (Fe, Al, Ca, Si) of bulk sediment samples; C and N of heavy fraction; and extractable OC, Fe, and Al, and organic matter characterization using high-resolution mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS) of sequential extractions. Sample locations are included in the ‘sample_metadata.xlsx” file. Sediment characterization data is included in the accompanying csv files: bulk and density fractions (MCB2017_density-and-bulk-fractions.csv), sequential extractions (MCB2017_sequential-extractions.csv), and FT-ICR-MS data from sequential extractions in three files to be read by the R package ftmsRanalysis (MCB2017_FTICRMS-sequential-edata.csv, MCB2017_FTICRMS-sequential-emeta.csv, and MCB2017_FTICRMS-sequential-fdata.csv). Sediment was collected in triplicate; ID’s refer to individual samples.

measurementTechnique:
Methods provided below and also in the following publication: Anderson, C., Goebel, G., Tfaily, M., Fox, P., Nico, P., Fendorf, S., Keiluweit, M. Molecular nature of mineral-organic associations within redox-active mountainous floodplain sediments. ACS Earth Space Chem. In Review.
Sediment sampling:
We collected sediment samples in triplicate in June 2017 at three positions along the sampling transect, at shallow (30 cm) and deep depths (70 cm) (Fig. 1, Table S2); these depths were chosen based on visual assessment of sediment redoximorphic features during field sampling. Sediments were air-dried and sieved to 2 mm. Sediments across the transect dry out to 27-59% volumetric water content upon drainage in September (Table S1); thus precipitation of redox-active metal phases may have occurred during sample processes and the data reported here likely represent the state of mineral-organic associations present within the sediments during fully drained, oxic periods spanning from mid-summer to the following spring. No unexpected or unusually high safety hazards were encountered in the sampling and subsequent analysis of sediment samples.
Bulk sediment characterization:
We determined total sediment carbon and nitrogen in triplicate using an ECS 4010 CHNS-O elemental analyzer (Costech Analytical Technologies, Inc., Valencia, CA, USA). We measured total metals (Fe, Al, Ca, Si, etc.) on finely ground samples using X-ray fluorescence (Spectro Xepos HE XRF Spectrometer). We determined sediment texture after loss on ignition to remove organic matter (4 h at 550 C) by a laser diffraction particle size analyzer (Beckman Coulter LS 13 320, Indianapolis, IN). We estimated root biomass by picking out coarse roots from air dried sediments. Analytical error was orders of magnitude lower than the variance among replicates, and thus only standard error of the means of replicates are reported.
Density fractionation and carbon content:
To isolate organic matter of decreasing bioavailability (e.g., particulate to mineral-associated organic matter), we used a density fractionation procedure modified from the literature (Hatton et al., 2012; Keiluweit et al., 2018). Briefly, two sodium polytungstate (SPT) solutions were prepared in DI water at the following densities: 1.6 g cm3 and 2.2 g cm3 (solutions #1 and #2, respectively). Particulate organic matter was determined by adding and gently vortexing 30 ml of solution #1 and 7.5 g of sediment, shaking for 2 h at low speed, and centrifuging for 1 h at 1000 x g. The supernatant was filtered (0.8 μm, Millipore), rinsed thoroughly with DI water to remove excess SPT, and the filter was oven-dried at 60 C and weighed to determine the amount of particulate organic matter. To determine the intermediate density fraction (> 1.6 and < 2.2 cm3), 30 ml of solution #2 was added to the remaining sediment pellet, and the above steps were repeated. The final density fraction (> 2.2 g cm3) was determined by thoroughly cleaning the remaining sediment pellet with DI water. 30 ml of DI water was added and vortexed until the pellet was suspended, then centrifuged for 1 h at 2000 x g. The supernatant was removed, and this process was repeated three times. The dry mass of the remaining sediment pellet was recorded. The intermediate and heavy fractions together comprised the MAOC pool. We determined carbon and nitrogen content of density fractions in triplicate as described above for bulk sediment.
Sequential extractions:
To selectively dissolve mineral phases of varying degrees of order and their associated organic matter, sediments were extracted sequentially with four reagents (Fox et al., 2017; Heckman et al., 2018; Wagai and Mayer, 2007). After each extraction, the supernatant was filtered using 0.22 μm filters (Sigma-Aldrich). Briefly, 0.33 g sediment was extracted with 10 ml deionized (DI) water to extract bioavailable phases of minerals and organic matter (shaken 2 h at 200 rpm, centrifuged 20 min at 510 x g); this extraction represented water-extractable organic carbon (WEOC). The same pellet was then extracted with 10 ml of 0.1 M sodium pyrophosphate to target amorphous metal-organic complexes(Heckman et al., 2018; Kaiser et al., 2016) (shaken 16 h at 200 rpm, centrifuged 1 h at 4000 x g) and combined with the filtered extract of a 6.7 ml DI water rinse (shaken 2 h at 200 rpm, centrifuged 1 h at 4000 x g). Then, 10 ml of 0.5 M hydrochloric acid (HCl) was added to the remaining pellet to target short-range order phases (Fox et al., 2017) (shaken 4 h at 200 rpm, centrifuged 20 min 4000 x g) and combined with the filtered extract of a 6.7 ml DI water rinse (shaken 2 h at 200 rpm, centrifuged 20 min at 510 x g). Lastly, 10 ml of 0.049 M sodium dithionite was added to the pellet to target total reducible oxide phases (Wagai and Mayer, 2007) (shaken 16 h at 200 rpm, centrifuged 20 min at 510 x g) and combined with the filtered extract of a 6.7 ml of 0.05 M HCl rinse (shaken 1 h at 200 rpm, centrifuged 20 min at 510 x g).
Metal and TOC analysis of sequential extractions:
Extracts were analyzed for metals using Microwave Plasma-Atomic Emission Spectrometry (Agilent, Santa Clara, CA), diluting to a final concentration of 2% nitric acid. Extracts were analyzed for total organic carbon using a TOC-L Analyzer (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan), diluting in DI water.
Fourier-transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS) analysis of sequential extractions:
Extracts were analyzed for organic matter composition using a 12 Tesla Bruker SolariX FTICR spectrometer located at the Environmental Molecular Science Laboratory in Richland, WA. Samples were first desalted and concentrated using solid phase extraction (Dittmar et al., 2008) with bond elute PPL cartridges. The analyte was eluted from the PPL cartridge in HPLC grade methanol and introduced directly to a standard Bruker electrospray ionization source operating in negative mode. The instrument was externally calibrated weekly to a mass accuracy of < 0.1 ppm using a tuning solution from Agilent. The ion accumulation time varied to account for differences in C concentration between samples. A Suwannee River Fulvic Acid standard, obtained from the International Humic Substance Society, was used as a control to monitor potential carryover from one sample to another and ensure instrument stability in day-to-day operation. The instrument was flushed between samples using a mixture of Milli-Q water and HPLC grade methanol. One hundred and forty-four individual scans were averaged for each sample and internally calibrated using OM homologous series separated by 14 Da (-CH2 groups). The mass measurement accuracy was < 1 ppm for singly charged ions across a broad mass-over-charge (m/z) range (i.e., 100 < m/z < 1100). The mass resolution was 350,000 at 339.112 Da. BrukerDaltonik data analysis software (version 4.2) was used to convert raw spectra to a list of m/z values applying FT-MS peak picker module with a signal‐to‐noise ratio threshold of 7 and absolute intensity threshold of 100. Formularity software (Tolić et al., 2017) was used to assign chemical formulae based on the criteria previously described (Tfaily et al., 2018). Peaks were filtered to only include masses between 200 < m/z < 900. Compounds were grouped into molecular classes (e.g., lipid-, protein-, carbohydrate-, lignin-, tannin-, condensed aromatic-like) based on C, H, and O for H/C and O/C ranges according to previous literature (Bailey et al., 2017) . Each assigned molecular formula was used to calculate the nominal oxidation state of C (NOSC), double bond equivalence (DBE), and aromaticity index (AI) as in previous work (LaCroix et al., 2019).
